title: Jagannath's summer fever
hookLine: every summer, after a grand bath, the god of Puri falls ill and is nursed out of sight: why Hindus serve God like family
carry: murti seva: god is cared for like family
tomorrow: who holds the hill when it rains?

lines: A BATH IN FRONT OF THE CROWDS.
cards: The hottest month of the year in Puri, on India's east coast.

On the full moon, the temple's three great wooden deities, Jagannath, his brother Balabhadra and his sister Subhadra, are carried out to a high platform in front of huge crowds and bathed with pot after pot of cool water.
It's a loud, joyful day. And then, tradition says, they catch a fever. Today, the god who gets sick in summer.

teach.b: After the bathing festival, Snana Purnima, the temple's inner doors close to the public for about two weeks. In Puri's tradition this is anasara: the deities are said to be unwell, and they rest out of sight.
Their own hereditary servants nurse them with herbal medicines and simple offerings instead of the usual feasts, until they recover.
Then they appear again, freshly painted, and soon after ride out in their great chariots for the Ratha Yatra. Charaka would recognize the care.
His summer chapter says the strong sun draws moisture out of the body, so you meet it with cool water, light food and rest. But the teaching here is bigger than health.

teach.h: MURTI SEVA: GOD SERVED LIKE FAMILY
teach.b: Hindus treat a consecrated image, a murti, not as a statue but as a presence: God invited in and served the way you'd serve a beloved guest or a family member.

So the deity is woken in the morning, bathed, dressed, fed, and put to rest at night, and in Puri, even nursed through a fever. That's murti seva, service to God in the image. You see it in ordinary homes too.

teach.h: COTTON CLOTHES AND A SMALL FAN
teach.b: In summer many families dress their home deity in light cotton, offer cooling food and water, and some set a small fan by the shrine. To an outsider it can look like pretend.
To a devotee it's love that pays attention, the way you'd notice a grandparent getting too warm. In this teaching God isn't only far away. He's close enough to be looked after.

how: At Puri, Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra are bathed on Snana Purnima and then rest out of public sight for about two weeks, nursed with herbal medicines; in summer many Hindu families dress their home deity in light cotton and offer cooling food and water. People who follow Ayurveda keep cool with sweet, cool, liquid food and rest.

a statue cleaned once a year for the visitors

games.why: murti seva treats God in the image as present and loved. even Jagannath, in Puri, is nursed through his summer fever.

practice: Bring your attention to the tip of the nose and notice that the in-breath is a little cooler there than the out-breath; rest on the cool of each inhale.
Then picture one small act of care you could give today, a glass of cold water, a fan turned toward someone. If you pray, offer a little water at your family's shrine, as many Hindus do in the heat.
If you don't, offer it to someone thirsty.

wordCard.voice: The seasons. In summer, Charaka's sun draws moisture out and cool water puts it back, and in Puri, God himself is bathed, rests and is nursed through the heat. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: murti, a form or image. A consecrated murti is served in Hindu worship as God present.

carryVoice: Your line: murti seva, God is cared for like family, even through a summer fever. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Jagannath temple tradition, Puri (Snana Purnima on the full moon of Jyeshtha; anasara, the deities' rest out of public view, tended with herbal medicines by their hereditary servants; reappearance before Ratha Yatra)
Murti seva (daily service of a consecrated image as a living presence: waking, bathing, dressing, offering food, rest; seasonal changes in home worship)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6 (grishma: the sun draws out moisture; sweet, cold, liquid food and drink; avoid exertion; rest, cool places)
